questions.question: Linezolid

parts.text: What class of antibiotic is it?
Describe its mechanism of action
What are 2 health canada approved indications
What clinical disease must be monitored for if he were also taking Sertraline

questions.model_answer:
a) Class: oxazolidinone.
b) Mechanism of action: binds the 23S ribosomal RNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing formation of the 70S initiation complex and blocking bacterial protein synthesis initiation (bacteriostatic against most organisms).
c) Two approved indications: (1) complicated/uncomplicated skin and skin-structure infections caused by susceptible gram-positive organisms (MRSA/MSSA, S. pyogenes) (2) vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium infections (nosocomial or community-acquired pneumonia due to S. pneumoniae/S. aureus is another accepted answer).
d) With concurrent sertraline: monitor for serotonin syndrome - linezolid is a reversible, nonselective monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and combination with a serotonergic agent (SSRI) can precipitate serotonin syndrome (fever, agitation, altered mental status, tremor).

parts.text: List 4 possible drug interactions (antibiotic, other drug, interaction)

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin-Rivaroxaban: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of rivaroxaban. Rifampin-Sertraline: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration of sertraline. Rifampin-Bisoprolol/Perindopril/Amlodipine: CYP3A4 strong inducers may decrease serum concentration. Linezolid-Metformin: MAOIs may enhance hypoglycemic effect. Linezolid-Sertraline: linezolid may enhance serotonergic effect of SSRIs, risk of serotonin syndrome. Ciprofloxacin-Metformin: quinolones may enhance/diminish hypoglycemic effect. questions.question: Q5 (2016 AM) Linezolid

parts.text: a) What is the dose of Linezolid for a 70kg with CrCl 20 for MRSA bacteremia
b) He develops rigors, fever, agitation. What is the cause?
c) What are 3 hematologic complications which develop from Linezolid in order of most to least common?

cohort_answer.text: a) 600mg IV q12h (normal dose regardless of renal function - no adjustment for renal impairment, PD, CRRT etc). b) Serotonin syndrome - linezolid is a reversible, nonselective MAOI; fever, agitation, mental status changes, tremors, autonomic hyperactivity; avoid co-admin with alcohol, amphetamines, methadone, MAOI, TCA, SSRI; monitor with antipsychotics. c) Thrombocytopenia (most common, ~47% after 10 days, immune mediated) > Anemia (bone marrow suppression) > Leukopenia (least common, in pediatrics order is Anemia > Leukopenia = Thrombocytopenia).

questions.question: Linezolid

parts.text: What is the class?
What are the approved indications?
What percent bioavailable is the oral formulation?
Does it require renal-dose adjustment in renal disease?

questions.model_answer:
a) Class: oxazolidinone.
b) Approved indications: nosocomial and community-acquired pneumonia due to susceptible S. aureus (MRSA/MSSA) or S. pneumoniae; complicated and uncomplicated skin/skin-structure infections due to S. aureus, S. pyogenes, or S. agalactiae; and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium infections.
c) Oral bioavailability: approximately 100%.
d) Renal-dose adjustment: not required - linezolid does not require dose adjustment in renal impairment or on dialysis (standard 600 mg q12h dosing is used regardless of renal function).

questions.question: Q4 (2006 AM): Daptomycin and Linezolid

parts.text: A) Give 2 similarities in pharmacokinetic and spectrum
B) Give 2 differences in the same things

cohort_answer.text: A) Only PK similarity: renal excretion (30% linezolid, ~80% daptomycin). Spectrum: gram positive coverage incl MRSA, VRE. B) Protein binding: Dapto 90% vs Linezolid 31%. CNS penetration: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Pneumonia: Dapto poor vs Linezolid adequate. Spectrum: Dapto GP only, no mycobacteria vs Linezolid broad GP coverage, mycobacteria covered. Practicality: Dapto IV only, wt based, renal dosing vs Linezolid PO/IV, fixed dose, no renal dosing, high bioavailability.

questions.question: Q6 (2004 AM) Linezolid

parts.text: a) Mechanism of action
b) Organisms covered
c) Indications
d) advantages, disadvantages
e) Potential complications

cohort_answer.text: a) Binds bacterial 23S ribosomal RNA of 50S subunit, preventing 70S initiation complex formation, inhibiting protein synthesis. b) Gram positives: Staphylococci, Streptococci, Enterococci, and others (Corynebacterium, Listeria, Bacillus, Micrococcus, Erysipelothrix, Leuconostoc, Rhodococcus equi, Pediococcus, Actinomyces); Gram negative: in vitro activity against Pasteurella multocida, Fusobacterium, Capnocytophaga, Moraxella catarrhalis, Legionella, Bordetella, Elizabethkingia meningoseptica, moderate vs H. influenzae; Mycobacteria: TB, NTM; inhibits toxin production in staph/strep. c) FDA approved: VRE infections incl bacteremia; nosocomial pneumonia (S. aureus MSSA/MRSA, S. pneumoniae incl MDR); complicated SSTI incl diabetic foot without OM (S. aureus MSSA/MRSA, S. pyogenes, S. agalactiae); uncomplicated SSTI (MSSA only, S. pyogenes); CAP (S. pneumoniae incl MDR, or MSSA only). d) Advantages: near 100% bioavailability, oral formulation, no renal dosing, CNS/lung penetration, anti-toxin effect. Disadvantages: serotonin syndrome risk, price, increased mortality in catheter-related infections with GN/mixed/unknown organisms, cytopenias/lactic acidosis/neuropathy, bacteriostatic (except vs strep). e) Hematologic (thrombocytopenia, anemia, leukopenia); Neurological (mitochondrial toxicity, neuropathies, optic neuropathy, hand dysesthesia); lactic acidosis; serotonin syndrome; GI (N/V/D).

questions.question: Describe the specific mechanisms of actions for the following anti-tubercular medications.

parts.text: Isoniazid
Rifamycins
Linezolid
Levofloxacin
Bedaquiline

questions.model_answer: Isoniazid: a prodrug activated by mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase (KatG); the activated form inhibits InhA, blocking mycolic acid synthesis and disrupting the mycobacterial cell wall. Rifamycins: inhibit the beta-subunit of DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB), blocking bacterial RNA transcription. Linezolid: binds the 23S rRNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing formation of the 70S initiation complex and inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. Levofloxacin: inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, preventing DNA supercoiling/replication. Bedaquiline: inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, depleting intracellular ATP and producing bactericidal activity over several days.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 481, 484, 490, 493-494 (mechanisms of isoniazid, rifamycins, linezolid, fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline)

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Linezolid, Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline.

parts.text: Rifampin
Isoniazid
Linezolid
Moxifloxacin
Bedaquiline

cohort_answer.text: Rifampin: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase, occurring as a result of drug binding in the polymerase subunit deep within the DNA/RNA channel, facilitating direct blocking of elongating RNA. Isoniazid: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis, interfering with cell wall synthesis, producing a bactericidal effect; also disrupts DNA, lipid, carbohydrate, and NAD synthesis/metabolism. Linezolid: Inhibits initiation of bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S rRNA component of the 50S ribosome (contains 5S rRNA, 23S rRNA, 34 proteins); also suppresses production of bacterial toxins such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, alpha-hemolysin, and TSST-1. Moxifloxacin: Directly inhibits DNA synthesis; binds to DNA gyrase and DNA topoisomerase IV, generating DNA cleavage. Bedaquiline: Inhibits bacterial ATP synthase; ATP production is required for cellular energy production and its loss leads to inhibition of mycobacterial growth within hours
